newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Supply ship docks with Mir, unloading on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Supply ship docks with Mir, unloading on Tuesday.

text.p: A supply ship successfully docked with Russia's Mir space station on Monday in a tricky operation crucial for the future of the troubled 11-year-old mission.

The unmanned Progress craft was carrying oxygen, food, water and tools required to carry out repairs in the Spektr module, badly damaged on June 25 when another supply ship ploughed into the ageing space station.

But a spokeswoman at the Mission Control centre just outside Moscow said the unloading of the equipment had been postponed until Tuesday because of the need to recharge the batteries of the Kvant module, where Progress had been docked.
Kvant and Spektr are two of a series of separate sections assembled in space to make up Mir, which is the focus of Moscow's space programme.
Earlier deputy flight director Viktor Blagov had said the unloading would take place on Monday evening.
"Now the crew is sleeping. The hatch will be opened tomorrow," the spokeswoman said. She gave no further details.
The sprawling space station was directly over the Volga river in Russia on its orbit round the Earth when the docking took place.
Also aboard the Progress craft are parcels from the families of the three-man Russian-U.S. crew, who have had a nerve-wracking and uncomfortable time since the accident.
British-born American Michael Foale lost all his belongings in the collision and asked NASA to send him a new toothbrush.
During Mission Control's communication with the crew on Monday a senior doctor, Igor Goncharov, urged them to avoid exerting themselves too much during the unloading of Progress.
"You are doing an excellent job but the volume of your work will also increase," Goncharov said.

He also advised them to get plenty of rest and to take lots of vitamins in the coming days as they prepare for their sortie to the holed module to reconnect electrical cables and restore some power lost after the collision.
The two Russian cosmonauts, Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, will make the trip to Spektr in heavy protective spacesuits, probably around July 18 though no final date has been fixed.

"We have come to the conclusion that the cosmonauts may not have to fully enter the module. It is possible they could do the work halfway inside Spektr and halfway in the hatch," deputy flight director Sergei Krikalyov told reporters on Monday.
"The cosmonauts have been checking out their spacesuits but have not worked in them yet," he added.
Their American colleague, Michael Foale, will sit in the escape capsule for safety during the sortie, which is expected to last up to four hours.

At the weekend Russian and NASA officials in the United States said there had been a mystery leak into space from the holed Spektr module after the collision. Krikalyov said there were no leaks of any kind on the ageing space station now.
But he said that the cosmonauts had reported seeing a "white-coloured cloud" two days after the collision coming from the direction of Spektr.
"We do not have a reason for the cloud," he said, adding that it might have been a substance that had escaped from the crew's medical supplies stored in the damaged module.
Another theory was that the crew had seen ammonium which had escaped from the cooling system after the collision, he said.
Confirming an earlier report, Krikalyov said the cosmonauts had also heard a "light thump" before sighting the apparent leakage.
A NASA official said on Sunday the decision whether to send a replacement U.S. astronaut to Mir in September would rest on the assignment's likelihood of being safe and productive.
Navy Cmdr. Wendy Lawrence, 37, is slated to begin a four-month stay on Mir in September, replacing Foale, the fifth NASA astronaut to live and work on the station.
